item.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
item.description:
Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park

A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon.

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

item.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
item.description:
Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections

The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

item.dc:creator: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg

item.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
item.description:
Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa

When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.

“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”

item.title: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
item.description:
Ukraine’s security service says seven drones were launched from mothership in operation that sank Merkury warship

Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.

Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.

item.title: Russian warship sinks in Benghazi after suspected Ukrainian drone attack
item.description:
No one has claimed responsibility for the strike on the vessel, which had docked on its way back to Russia

A Russian warship docked in the Libyan port city of Benghazi was struck in the early hours of Sunday in a suspected Ukrainian sea drone attack, causing a dramatic night-time explosion and the sinking of the vessel.

The strike severely damaged the Merkury, a Russian navy corvette that had stopped to refuel and take on supplies, according to Libyan officials from the country’s eastern government.

item.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, police say
item.description:
Unclear if ‘hostage-taker’ who was killed may have been a hostage as daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre ends

Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one man police described as a hostage-taker was killed.

Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.

item.dc:creator: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent

item.title: Lululemon founder stuns Canadian women’s leadership conference with sexist comments
item.description:
Chip Wilson said men importing brides from Thailand was due to women waiting too long to have children

The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand, in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference.

Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it aims to create space for “candid conversations about the barriers women face both in business and society”.

item.title: Colombia’s president arrives at scene of supermarket hostage siege in tourist city
item.description:
Abelardo de la Espriella to take control of operation trying to free at least 20 hostages

Colombia’s president has arrived at the scene of an hours-long standoff between security services and gunmen holding at least 20 people hostage inside a supermarket in Cartagena, a popular tourist city.

Abelardo de la Espriella’s motorcade arrived in Cartagena on Tuesday night, Agence France-Presse reported, where he will ostensibly take control of an operation involving scores of officers, the navy and special forces.

item.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, man at center of Trump deportation battle, leaves US
item.description:
Salvadorian man, who was deported in March 2025 and returned to US after supreme court ruling, leaving of own volition for Spain

Kilmar Ábrego García has left the United States of his own volition, his lawyers confirmed on Tuesday, with the Department of Homeland Security confirming that he was travelling to Spain.

A source close to Ábrego said Madrid was his first stop but that it would not be his final destination.

item.title: Canada says it ‘does not report to the US’ after Pentagon criticizes military spending
item.description:
Scathing US document memo supposedly ‘atrophied’ defence capabilities of its northern neighbour

Canada is a “sovereign nation” that does not “report” to the United States, the country’s defense minister said after the Pentagon released a scathing memo that criticized the supposedly “atrophied” defence capabilities of its northern neighbour.

The document, released on Tuesday, said Canada had “yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs” necessary to meet previous defence spending pledges and become a “credible partner in the defense of our shared continent”.

item.title: China sends first foreign astronaut to ISS rival as it globalises space operations
item.description:
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station

China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

item.title: UK embassy in Japan warns of rise in drink spiking and credit card fraud at Tokyo bars
item.description:
Social media campaign fronted by British rapper Shao Dow advises tourists not to let their guard down

The British embassy in Tokyo has launched a social media campaign warning visitors to exercise caution after a rise in cases of drink-spiking and credit card fraud against tourists in the Japanese capital.

In a recent clip made in conjunction with the embassy, the British rapper and manga artist Shao Dow, a frequent visitor to Japan, notes that although the country “is incredibly safe, that doesn’t mean you can let your guard down”.

item.title: China misusing Interpol to target dissidents, says leading UK lawyer
item.description:
Concerns over Beijing’s use of ‘red notices’ as Hong Kong prepares to host police organisation’s general assembly

China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading British lawyer has claimed, as Hong Kong prepares to host the police organisation’s general assembly for the first time.

Ben Keith, a specialist in “red notices” - the Interpol system under which national authorities are requested to locate and detain suspects - said he was working on five cases involving China making questionable requests through Interpol.

item.title: China investigates politburo star in Xi Jinping’s latest purge
item.description:
Chen Jining, regarded as a contender for higher office, becomes the fourth member of China’s elite politburo to be investigated since 2025

China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s Communist party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s elite politburo, the state-run Xinhua news agency unexpectedly announced on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership ⁠body to be probed since ⁠2025.

China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating ​Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Xinhua said, using a common euphemism for corruption.

item.title: The Nvidia case is just the latest episode of Trump disregarding intelligence
item.description:
Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran

Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view.

Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang, was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geostrategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race.

item.title: Australian politics live: Hanson ‘delighted’ as Liberal senator defects to One Nation; Bowen says global tensions ‘infected’ Cop31
item.description:
• Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Pauline Hanson has released a statement this morning welcoming South Australian senator Leah Blyth to her party.

Blyth is the second high-profile federal defection from the Coalition to One Nation – after Barnaby Joyce.

Senator Blyth will be One Nation’s first South Australian Senator and will build on One Nation’s expanding support within the state.

My team and I are delighted to welcome Senator Blyth to sit in the Senate with One Nation.

We are facing at the next election clearly a coalition of the Liberals, Nationals and One Nation, with all the baggage that each of these parties brings to the table. They’re all anti-worker, they’re all extreme … this demonstrates, I think, more disunity in the Liberal party under Angus Taylor.

item.description:
Fire making a ‘significant run’ towards the southwest of the island on Thursday, Tasmania Fire Service says

Homes and properties on a picturesque remote island remain under threat from an out-of-control bushfire that has sent smoke hundreds of kilometres south.

The blaze on Flinders Island in Bass Strait spread significantly on Wednesday after being started by lightning strikes.

item.title: Liberal senator Leah Blyth announces defection to One Nation
item.description:
South Australian senator labels One Nation the ‘only party with the bold ideas needed to turn this country around’

Leah Blyth, federal Liberal senator for South Australia, has announced she is defecting to One Nation, becoming the party’s first upper-house member for the state.

Blyth, a member of Angus Taylor’s frontbench, said she did not believe the Coalition was capable of opposing the Albanese government, which was “running the country into the ground”.

item.title: Aidan is one of thousands of students forced to verbally defend his honours thesis as universities take on AI
item.description:
Honours students are increasingly being asked to sit oral assessments – but at the University of Sydney it’s become a requirement for all

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

When Aidan Elwig Pollock signed up for an honours program at the University of Sydney, he did not expect his 20,000-word thesis to be accompanied by a spoken component.

But, as AI increasingly makes written research an unreliable form of assessment, the university has demanded all students taking the one-year program defend their arguments in conversation with professors.

item.title: IVF, elective abortion, gender-affirming care and VAD to cease under Catholic ownership of private hospitals
item.description:
ACCC approves Calvary’s takeover of 14 hospitals around Australia, with critics concerned move will add to pressures on public health system

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Advocates say access to voluntary assisted dying, IVF, elective abortions and gender-affirming care is under threat after the competition watchdog approved the takeover of 14 private hospitals by a Catholic healthcare provider.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) announced on Wednesday it had approved the takeover of the private hospitals by not-for-profit Catholic healthcare operator Calvary from collapsed provider Healthscope.

item.description:
Ábrego García chooses to depart from US after previously being deported to El Salvador due to ‘administrative error’

  • US politics – live updates

Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadorian national whose mistaken deportation turned him into a symbol of Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts, has landed in Spain.

Ábrego García arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after leaving the United States of his own volition.

item.title: EU nationals will pay higher tuition fees than UK students, Burnham indicates
item.description:
Asked by Kemi Badenoch to rule out equal rate for UK and EU students, PM says proposal ‘will not be put on the table’

European students will have to pay higher fees than their domestic equivalents at UK universities under a still-to-be-finalised part of the new deal with the EU, Andy Burnham has indicated.

The issue of fees paid by EU nationals studying at British universities is the main element of the arrangement hailed by Burnham in Brussels on Friday that has not been agreed, with both sides giving an extra six months to reach a solution.

item.title: ‘Russia wants more than Ukraine,’ Germany’s Merz warns – as it happened
item.description:
German chancellor, in wide-ranging speech, says Moscow is ‘escalating on a massive scale’

If you want to hear more about the new death toll, listen to today’s Today in Focus podcast with our Russia expert, Pjotr Sauer.

“Two groups of hackers accessed Russia’s main statistics database last month and discovered a cache of 11m death certificates that revealed nearly 500,000 Russian losses in Ukraine since 2022. Among these were 1,000 – the equivalent of a whole regiment – who took their own lives.

The documents show how the majority of soldiers come from poorer areas and ethnic minorities, drawn in by high salaries. There are also recruits from abroad and even those lured to Russia by offers of jobs. But for how long can Vladimir Putin keep this shocking death toll from the Russian people?”

item.title: Brussels on split-screen: where it flexes – and where it bends
item.description:
From a choreographed summit that dominated Westminster but barely registered in Brussels to a climate showdown in Turkey, last week revealed the EU’s priorities – and the limits of its collective power

• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

Two very different European diplomatic dramas played out almost simultaneously last week. On Friday, a tightly choreographed EU-UK summit transfixed London, while barely registering on the continent. On Sunday, Cop31 collapsed after a united EU forcefully vetoed a watered-down climate pact, even as it relaxed its own green rules at home.

What do these two events reveal about the EU: how it works, what takes up its bandwidth, how it exercises its clout – and where it’s vulnerable?

***

item.title: Number of women killed by men in Ireland almost doubles in a year
item.description:
Figures from past 30 years show more than half of victims killed by current or ex-partner

The number of women in Ireland killed by men has surged in the past five years and risen especially sharply in the past 12 months, according to a study.

After falling for two decades, the number of violent deaths began going up in 2021 and has risen sharply this year, with 13 deaths so far, the report by Irish charity Women’s Aid said on Wednesday.

item.title: UN sacked Palestinian staff on back of unproven Israeli allegations, tribunal rules
item.description:
Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged

A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

Continue reading...
item.dc:creator: Julian Borger Senior international correspondent

item.title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
item.description:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, at center of legal fight, says he ‘should not be unjustly accused’ because of leftwing views

James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

item.title: ‘They don’t believe in freedom’: Yemenis plan their escape as Houthis advance on Aden
item.description:
With Iran’s proxy fighters encircling the temporary capital, residents and NGOs prepare to evacuate

Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far south as he could to the port city of Aden, where there was a measure of safety.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government had made the city its temporary capital; the hundreds of kilometres between it and the Houthis were well fortified.

item.title: Israel attempts to jail Palestinian student at Hebrew University without trial
item.description:
Mahdi Tounsi appeared to have suffered maltreatment at hearing where he was not allowed to hear prosecution case against him

Palestinian student Mahdi Tounsi appeared in a closed-door court hearing in Jerusalem, as academics and activists warned that Israel’s attempt to jail him without trial marked a serious escalation in attacks on Palestinian rights.

Yael Berda, a lawyer and sociology professor at Hebrew University, who has taught Tounsi for four years, came to court to call for his release.

item.title: Gaza issues meningitis epidemic alert after steep rise in cases
item.description:
Health ministry records 272 new infections in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate

Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.

Dr Nidal Ghoneim, a senior official at the ministry, said the spread of the disease posed a threat to the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, including children.

item.title: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
item.description:
Officials at Delhi airport stopped Saurav Das from boarding flight to Britain, where students have invited him to speak

A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi high court to give him permission to fly to the UK after immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him boarding a flight early on Tuesday morning.

The court is scheduled to hear Saurav Das’s case on Thursday morning. His lawyer asked the court for a quick hearing because Das has by now already missed some of his engagements at British universities and can only attend the other events on his itinerary if he is allowed to fly out as soon as possible.

item.title: World Chess Championship 2026 Game 1: Gukesh Dommaraju and Javokhir Sindarov play to 38-move draw – as it happened
item.description:
• Sindarov and Gukesh play to 38-move draw in Game 1

  • Explainer: all your pre-match questions, answered

  • Sindarov interview: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’

  • Play through 22 famous world championship games

The players have shaken hands and we’re off! We have a Berlin defense of the Ruy Lopez (1 e4 e5 2 Nf3 Nc6 3 Bb5 Nf6), one of the most thoroughly analyzed openings in modern chess.

The Berlin famously helped Vladimir Kramnik dethrone Garry Kasparov in their 2000 world title match in London and has been a staple of elite chess ever since, earning a reputation as one of black’s most reliable weapons against 1 e4.

item.title: Leader of India’s Cockroach movement says he was stopped from boarding flight to UK
item.description:
Saurav Das was due to give talks at UK universities on protest movement but says ‘coward government’ prevented him flying

A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has said he was prevented from leaving Delhi to fly to the UK to give talks on the viral group’s protests.

Saurav Das, 27, has been at the forefront of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which has amassed millions of social media followers since its launch in May. Das, who was due to fly out early on Tuesday, said immigration officials told him at the airport that his passport had been flagged.

item.title: After 80 years in Oxford, Naga ancestors are finally going home
item.description:
A campaign securing the landmark return to India of ancestral remains taken during British colonial rule has opened a wider conversation about restitution

• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

The lacerating legacy of colonialism survives in many spaces, particularly in museum collections and private holdings across the western world. And it’s not just limited to inanimate artefacts or cultural objects.

For almost 80 years, human remains were displayed on crowded glass shelves at Pitt Rivers Museum at Oxford University, one of the world’s most celebrated institutions.

item.title: Myanmar has been found guilty of genocide. Should Israel be worried? – podcast
item.description:
The international court of justice has for the first time ruled that a state has committed genocide. Yasmin Ullah explains what it means for the Rohingya people, while Kaamil Ahmed lays out how the case unfolded

For seven years, Yasmin Ullah had been part of the delegation arguing that Myanmar had committed genocide – one of the gravest human rights crimes – against Rohingya Muslims.

The genocide has directly affected Yasmin and her family. Last week she was in court to hear the international court of justice’s landmark verdict against Myanmar. “I was really kind of pinching myself. It felt like we were all able to breathe again,” she tells Annie Kelly.

item.title: Andy Taylor, guitarist in Duran Duran, dies aged 65
item.description:
Musician who had huge 1980s chart success had been diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2018

Andy Taylor, the guitarist with 80s pop megastars Duran Duran, has died aged 65.

He had been diagnosed with stage four metastatic prostate cancer in 2018, which he disclosed publicly in 2022 when Duran Duran were about to be inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

item.title: Judge orders transfer of Thomas Markle to face formal charges in California
item.description:
Father of the Duchess of Sussex currently being held in Florida is charged with possession of child pornography

A judge in the US has ordered the transfer of Thomas Markle, the Duchess of Sussex’s father, to California to face formal charges of possessing child sex abuse images.

The move comes after a federal grand jury on the west coast paved the way for the prosecution of Markle Sr, who is currently being held in custody in Florida. He was charged with two counts of possession of child pornography.

item.title: UK food inflation could hit 5% next year, Bank of England says
item.description:
Sharp rise expected as cost pressures mount, with experts factoring in energy price cap hike and potential impact of El Niño

Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the Bank of England has said, despite rising less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war.

The deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee: “Food price inflation is coming in under what we expected [it] to be, and in fact under what the industry expected it to be.”

item.title: Ministers can’t control gas prices, but they can attack other energy costs more ruthlessly
item.description:
Louise Haigh talked the right talk at the CBI this week, but greater ambition and tighter timelines are needed

Shocked by average annual energy bills at £2,166 for the first three months of next year? Here’s worse news. It is currently possible, and perhaps even likely, that the regulator, Ofgem, will set the price cap at £2,000-plus in every quarter of 2027.

Predictions for bills are less certain the further out one looks, it should be said. Gas prices, the overwhelming culprit in the £443 hike in the cap announced on Wednesday, can always fall – and might do so if calm returns to the strait of Hormuz.

item.title: Treasury raises cost concerns over Milburn plan on youth unemployment
item.description:
Chancellor wants system laid out in Alan Milburn’s review to break even at an earlier date, sources say

The Treasury has raised concerns about the level of spending on support proposed in Alan Milburn’s review into youth unemployment, amid pressure for the welfare bill to start reducing more quickly.

Whitehall sources have told the Guardian that the chancellor, John Healey, is not happy with the level of spending required under the proposals and wants the system to break even at an earlier date.

item.title: New York City’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade postponed due to weather
item.description:
Forecasters say high winds on Thursday may spoil the annual march of huge balloons and have moved the parade to Saturday

New York City’s Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade has been postponed due to excessively windy weather and will now be held on Saturday.

Forecasters say an impending storm on Thursday may spoil the street party, which is marked by a march of huge balloons. AccuWeather is forecasting winds of 12 to 25 mph (19 to 40 km/h) and rain later on Thursday.

item.title: Oregon man and dog narrowly escape being swept away by high tides as officials urge caution at beaches
item.description:
Record-breaking king tides have prompted west coast authorities to warn residents to stay away from beaches

The US west coast has seen record-breaking tides this week and authorities have urged residents to avoid beaches, but not everyone is heeding those warnings.

In Cannon Beach, Oregon, viral footage showed a man and his dog nearly getting swept away by a so-called king tide on Tuesday morning. The man had been standing on a staircase holding his leashed dog, who was walking in the sand, when the water suddenly surged, knocking him to his feet.

item.title: High levels of salmonella found in some products from nation’s biggest turkey producer
item.description:
Two years of inspections at four Butterball plants show rates far exceeding US averages in ground or chopped meat

Inspectors found salmonella bacteria in more than a third of ground or chopped turkey samples at slaughterhouses owned by Butterball, the US’s biggest turkey company, data shows.

The US Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) food safety and inspection service (FSIS) and some states conduct regular checks for salmonella and other bacteria in commercial poultry plants. Salmonella can live in the intestines of poultry, and it can cause nausea, diarrhea and even death in humans if meat is not cooked properly and then consumed.

item.title: Vance says Jensen Huang doesn’t need pardon after Trump says ‘it’s an option’
item.description:
Vice-president says he supports reinstatement of Nvidia CEO after ‘assurances’ from top US officials was ‘under no investigation’

JD Vance said on Wednesday that Jensen Huang, the recently reinstalled Nvidia CEO, was never under criminal investigation and therefore did not need a pardon after Donald Trump said he would be open to offering one to the tech executive.

The vice-president told reporters he supported Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO after receiving “assurances” from the attorney general and other top US officials that Huang was “under no investigation”.
